strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: object removal that must also handle object effects (shadows, reflections), which prior diffusion-based removal methods handle implicitly or not at all.

The OBER dataset is a substantive contribution: hybrid camera-captured (2,875 counterfactual pairs with fixed cameras, following ObjectDrop) and simulated data (10,000 composites) with separate object and object-effect mask annotations and RGBA foregrounds. Table 4 shows it is the only public dataset combining object masks, effect masks, RGBA objects, and both shadow and reflection effects.

The evaluation design is relatively thoughtful: baselines are tested under both Object Mask and Object-Effect Mask conditions, two new benchmarks (OBER-Test with GT, OBER-Wild without GT) are introduced, and a user study (30 participants, Table 5) and qualitative comparisons on in-the-wild data (Fig. 14/15) supplement the metrics.

The ablations (Table 2) are well structured, isolating contributions of the mask loss, simulated data, and attention-guided fusion; attention-map analysis (Fig. 6) with recall curves supports the OEA mechanism's claim of localizing effects.

Appendix is extensive: insertion/movement applications, user-stroke robustness, dataset statistics, an honest limitations section (overlapping shadows, very large shadow regions), and a human-in-the-loop reflection collection strategy.
Overall the manuscript is clearly written and technically plausible; the input design (feeding the unmasked image instead of the masked image) is a sensible and well-argued choice.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is a material concern: ObjectClear is fine-tuned on its own OBER data and evaluated on OBER-Test (160 samples split from the same collection), while all baselines are evaluated zero-shot on data distributions they were never trained on. The very large gaps (e.g., PSNR 32.98 vs. 27.42 for Attentive Eraser) likely conflate in-domain training advantage with method quality. A comparison where baselines are fine-tuned on OBER (or ObjectClear evaluated on other methods' training distributions) is missing, making the headline SOTA claim hard to attribute.

The Attention-Guided Fusion step, which produces the largest single gain (PSNR 28.00 -> 32.98 in Table 2 (c) to (d)), blends the generated image with the original input by copying pixels outside the predicted effect region. On test sets where input and GT are pixel-aligned captured pairs, this trivially inflates PSNR/PSNR-BG/LPIPS, since most of the image is copied from the input. The metric improvements may substantially overstate generative quality; a purely generative evaluation (without fusion) on aligned benchmarks is needed to disentangle this.

The relative importance of the dataset versus the method is not separated convincingly. The paper's biggest wins plausibly come from curated paired data with effect annotations, yet no baseline is retrained on OBER to test whether e.g. RORem or Attentive Eraser also improves with the same data.

Effect masks are derived from pixel-wise differences above a threshold, which is sensitive to global illumination drift, noise, and subtle/soft shadows; the claim of 'precise' masks is asserted but no mask-quality analysis (e.g., IoU against human annotation) is provided. The simulation pipeline also assumes effects factorize via the alpha map in Eq. 1, which may not hold for interreflections and ambient occlusion.

Several relevant recent baselines (ObjectDrop, OmniPaint, OmniEraser, SmartEraser) are discussed but excluded from quantitative comparison, partially justified by open-source availability; at least ObjectDrop-style retraining baselines would strengthen the case.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the manuscript: no explicit statement that OBER or code will be released (critical given the dataset is the central contribution); the threshold used for effect-mask construction and several pipeline hyperparameters are unspecified.
Presentation errors: references [27] and [28] are duplicate LDM citations, and the GPT-4o claim in the introduction cites [27] incorrectly; minor typos ('stil', 'Object-Affect').

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: existing object removal methods handle the object itself but leave shadows/reflections and perturb the background. The explicit modeling of object-effect regions is a sensible framing.

The OBER dataset is a concrete, reusable contribution: hybrid captured+simulated data, separate object/object-effect masks, RGBA foregrounds, and two new benchmarks (OBER-Test, OBER-Wild), with a reasonably detailed construction pipeline (Fig. 2, Eq. 1) and a comparison to prior datasets (Table 4).

The evaluation is relatively thorough for this area: three test sets, two mask conditions for baselines, ablations (Table 2), a user study with 30 participants (Table 5), qualitative comparisons including user-stroke robustness, and an honest limitations section (Sec. C.5).

Attention-Guided Fusion is a practical inference-time trick that measurably improves background preservation (PSNR 28.00 -> 32.98 in Table 2), and the attention-map visualizations (Fig. 6, 12) support the claim that cross-attention localizes effects.
weaknesses: Fairness of the headline comparison is questionable. Attention-Guided Fusion copies original input pixels into the output outside the predicted attention region. This is essentially a copy-paste post-process that mechanically inflates PSNR/PSNR-BG/LPIPS, yet no baseline is granted an equivalent blending step; the ablation shows a large share of the reported gains comes from this trivially favorable operation rather than from generative quality. The paper should report metrics with and without fusion for baselines, or provide a fusion-equipped baseline.

The most striking results (e.g., 26.40 vs 22.49 PSNR, 0.0802 vs 0.1883 LPIPS on RORD-Val) are suspiciously large for this task, and are partly an artifact of the above blending plus training/evaluating on closely related data. OBER-Test comes from the same capture pipeline and distribution as the training data, so generalization claims rest mainly on the 300-image OBER-Wild, which has no ground truth and is evaluated only with the single reference-free ReMOVE metric.

Limited technical novelty on the modeling side. The method is SDXL-Inpainting fine-tuning plus (i) stacked text/visual embeddings in cross-attention, explicitly following PhotoMaker [16]/FastComposer [35], and (ii) an attention-mask loss adopted from prior attention-localization work [35, 23]. The main novelty is the dataset and the mask-difference-based effect-mask construction, which is a heuristic (pixel-difference thresholding) rather than a principled effect model.

Simulated data construction raises realism and potential leakage concerns. Eq. 1 derives alpha in the effect area as (Igt - Iin)/(Igt + eps), which treats the effect as a simple multiplicative/linear layer; shadows are not generally linear in this form, and compositing by shadow-direction clustering may produce distributional artifacts that the model learns to exploit. The train/test correlation between simulated compositing pipeline and the composite-style test scenarios is not analyzed.

Baselines may be under-tuned for the object-removal setting: generic inpainting models are prompted with 'an empty scene' per MULAN, and no baseline is fine-tuned on OBER or comparable data, so it is unclear how much of the gain comes from data access rather than architecture. The RORD-Val mask re-annotation protocol (manually augmenting a public benchmark) is described only briefly and its consistency is unverifiable.

Carelessness that undermines confidence: references [27] and [28] are identical duplicates; citation numbers are inconsistent in the text (SDXL-INP cited as [1] in tables but [24] in Sec. 4.1; DesignEdit as [10] vs [7]; CLIPAway as [7] vs [10]), suggesting table/text mismatches; the reflection-training supplement is a human-in-the-loop add-on of only 50 pairs whose impact is not separated in the ablation.
The insertion/movement applications (Sec. 4.3, A.2) are shown only qualitatively with no metrics or baselines, so the claimed extension is anecdotal.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: removing objects together with their visual effects (shadows, reflections), where most prior inpainting/removal methods fail. The explicit modeling of object-effect regions is a sensible framing.

The OBER dataset is a useful contribution: counterfactual camera-captured pairs with precise object and object-effect masks, a simulation pipeline producing RGBA foregrounds and multi-object composites, and two new benchmarks (OBER-Test, OBER-Wild). Table 4 provides a clear positioning against existing datasets.

Experiments are fairly extensive: evaluations on three test sets, two mask-condition settings for baselines (a fair-minded design), ablations of each component (L_mask, simulated data, AG Fusion), a 30-participant user study, user-stroke robustness tests, insertion/movement extensions, and an honest limitations section.

Attention-Guided Fusion is a simple but effective inference-time strategy for background preservation, and the ablation (Table 2, c vs. d) supports its contribution. The predicted attention maps qualitatively capture both objects and effects (Fig. 6).
The paper is generally well written and organized, with the appendix providing substantial supporting material.
weaknesses: Potential unfairness in the evaluation protocol. ObjectClear is trained on OBER and evaluated on OBER-Test, which is drawn from the same capture pipeline and distribution as its training data, while baselines are not trained on OBER. This in-domain advantage makes the very large OBER-Test margins (e.g., PSNR 32.98 vs. 25.70 for the best baseline) difficult to interpret as a like-for-like comparison. Results on RORD-Val partially mitigate this, but the paper does not discuss or control for the in-domain effect.

Attention-Guided Fusion copies original input pixels into all regions outside the predicted object-effect mask. Since ground truth differs from the input only in the object-effect region, this copy-paste step trivially inflates PSNR/PSNR-BG/LPIPS on any benchmark where the input is already close to GT. The PSNR jump from 28.00 to 32.98 in Table 2 (c) to (d) is likely dominated by this artifact rather than by better removal. A no-GT metric (e.g., ReMOVE) or human evaluation is the more reliable evidence, and the paper should isolate this effect.

Missing comparisons with several relevant recent methods discussed in the related work itself, e.g., SmartEraser [11], Erase Diffusion [19], ObjectDrop's model, OmniPaint [39], OmniEraser [33], and UniReal [4]. Only a subset (SDXL-INP, PowerPaint, BrushNet, CLIPAway, DesignEdit, FreeCompose, Attentive Eraser, RORem) is quantitatively compared.

The headline gains (LPIPS 0.0802 vs. ~0.18–0.29; CLIP distance 0.0350 vs. ~0.06) are large enough to warrant extra scrutiny, and the paper does not analyze failure modes quantitatively or report per-category breakdowns; the recall of 0.97 for the attention map is mentioned only in passing (Fig. 6) without precision or threshold details.

Several citation/reference errors undermine polish: refs [27] and [28] are duplicates (Rombach et al., CVPR 2022), yet [27] is cited in the introduction as an example of recent generative models 'such as GPT-4o'; [1] is a bare HuggingFace URL; DesignEdit is cited as [7] in Table 1 but [10] in the reference list (with the [7]/[10] labels swapped between table sections); 'Object-Affect Attention' typo on page 5. Eq. (1) also allows negative alpha values in the effect area (e.g., reflections brighter than the background), which is not addressed.

The camera-captured set is small (2,715 training pairs), and the simulation pipeline's realism assumptions (alpha blending, eight shadow-direction clusters, flat-surface placement) may limit transfer to complex lighting; the paper provides no quantitative evidence on the realism gap between simulated and captured data beyond the aggregate ablation.

Novelty of the method components is moderate: stacked text+visual embeddings for cross-attention follows PhotoMaker [16], the mask loss follows FastComposer [35]/PortraitBooth [23], and attention-guided blending is a natural extension of BrushNet-style fusion; the primary novelty rests on the dataset and the object-effect supervision, which should be stated more explicitly.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practical problem: removing both objects and their associated visual effects (shadows, reflections) while preserving background fidelity, which prior diffusion-based inpainting/removal methods demonstrably fail at (Fig. 1, 5, 7).

The OBER dataset is a significant contribution: a hybrid of 2,878 camera-captured counterfactual pairs and 10,000 simulated composites with precise object masks, object-effect masks, and RGBA foregrounds, plus two public benchmarks (OBER-Test, OBER-Wild). The comparison to existing datasets (Table 4) is thorough and the release commitment adds community value.

Experimental evaluation is unusually comprehensive: three primary test sets, additional external benchmarks (OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, MULAN in the supplementary), a 30-participant user study, efficiency comparison, and an ablation of each proposed component (Table 2).

The fairness analysis is careful and reassuring: baselines are evaluated under both object-mask and object-effect-mask conditions (Table 1), and supplementary Table 7 shows ObjectClear still outperforms all baselines even when they are given ground-truth object-effect masks for blending, addressing the concern that AGF's copy-paste blending drives the gains.
The SVDS observation (DS=1.0 causes color shift vs. DS=0.99 causing incomplete removal) is clearly diagnosed and the spatially-varying solution is simple and effective (Table 2 d–f, Fig. 11).
The method is efficient: 1.63 s/image at 512×512 on an A100, >5x faster than Flux-based competitors (OmniPaint, OmniEraser), while achieving better results.
Limitations are honestly discussed (Sec. 8.9, Fig. 17), including under-/over-removal of effects in scenes with overlapping shadows.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental. ATA is essentially a CLIP text+visual-embedding prompt with a mask-supervised attention loss on an SDXL-Inpainting backbone; AGF is attention-guided alpha blending of the input background; SVDS re-injects the background at a fixed denoising strength. Each component is a reasonable engineering choice but none is conceptually deep.

Much of the performance advantage appears data-centric rather than method-centric: the AGF step alone lifts PSNR from 28.04 to 32.77 (Table 2 c–d), and the largest gains occur on OBER-Test, a set drawn from the same capture and simulation pipeline as the training data (PSNR 33.04 vs. 29.06 for OmniPaint), which raises concerns about distribution-matched advantage. Gains on external benchmarks are much smaller (e.g., OmniPaint-Bench: 26.35 vs. 25.56 PSNR; LPIPS 0.0950 vs. 0.1001), suggesting the true state-of-the-art margin is modest.
OBER-Test contains only 163 samples with pixel-difference-threshold-derived masks, a small and potentially noisy evaluation set; key claims rest heavily on it alongside RORD-Val.
The OBER-Wild evaluation uses ReMOVE†, a self-modified version of an existing reference-free metric, which limits comparability and interpretability of those numbers.

All training and evaluation is at 512×512 (images downsampled and cropped), limiting assessment of high-resolution behavior and favoring comparisons over methods that natively operate at 1024 (OmniEraser results are resized down); the effect of this resizing protocol is not analyzed.

Eq. 2's L_mask formulation and the choice of SVDS constants (1.0 vs. 0.99) are presented empirically without sensitivity analysis; the motivation for the specific background DS=0.99 (other than citing prior usage) is thin.

Several implementation details relevant to reproducibility (e.g., the predefined threshold for effect-mask extraction, exact attention-map extraction layer, inference-time background re-injection mechanics) are underspecified in the main paper, though the supplementary mitigates some of this.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem (removing objects together with their shadows/reflections) and clearly articulates why prior inpainting/removal methods fail at this.

The OBER dataset with paired captured images, effect masks, and RGBA foregrounds is a concrete resource contribution; the hybrid captured/simulated pipeline and the promised public release add value for the community.

The experimental section is broad: comparisons under both object-mask and object-effect-mask conditions, ablations of each component (Table 2), additional external benchmarks (OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, MULAN in Tables 5-6), a user study, a fairness check giving baselines ground-truth effect masks for blending (Table 7), efficiency numbers, and an honest limitations section.

The paper is generally well written and the framework components (ATA, AGF, SVDS) are described in enough detail to follow, with training details and resolution/batch/learning-rate specifications provided.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. ObjectClear is a fine-tuned SDXL-Inpainting with (1) a simple mask-supervised cross-attention loss (Eq. 2 is a one-line mean-attention contrast), (2) an inference-time alpha-blend of the output with the input using a Gaussian-blurred attention map, and (3) a heuristic denoising-strength split (1.0 inside the mask, 0.99 outside). Attention-guidance ideas closely resemble existing work (Attentive Eraser, CLIPAway, BrushNet-style blending), and the individual components are engineering-level refinements rather than a new technique.

Evidence that AGF inflates the fidelity metrics. The large jump in Table 2 from (c) to (d) (PSNR 28.04 -> 32.77, PSNR-BG 28.80 -> 35.50) is driven by copying the input background back into the output, which by construction maximizes PSNR/PSNR-BG on the unchanged background. Although Table 7 shows baselines also improve when given GT masks for blending, this evaluation protocol still structurally favors a method whose headline numbers come partly from a copy-paste operation, and it makes the very large margins on OBER-Test (e.g., PSNR 33.04 vs. 29.06 for OmniPaint) difficult to interpret as pure generation quality.

Self-constructed evaluation data dominate the strongest claims. The most striking improvements are reported on OBER-Test, a benchmark built from the authors' own capture pipeline whose foreground objects are the very objects used to construct the training simulations; distributional overlap between training and test conditions is plausible and not analyzed. On external benchmarks (Tables 5-6) the margins over OmniPaint are much smaller (e.g., OmniPaint-Bench PSNR 26.35 vs. 25.56), which weakens the 'superior performance' narrative.

Questionable metric construction. For OBER-Wild the authors use ReMOVE†, a self-modified version of ReMOVE; introducing a modified reference-free metric for the only in-the-wild benchmark, without validation that the modification correlates with human judgment, is weakly supported. Notably, ObjectClear loses to OmniPaint on this metric (0.8470 vs. 0.8656) in Table 1 even as the text claims state-of-the-art on 'nearly all' metrics.

Dataset scale and diversity claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly calls OBER 'large-scale', but the physically captured portion is only 2,715 training pairs, and the 10,000 simulated images reuse foregrounds extracted from that same small captured set, so foreground diversity is bounded by 2,878 objects. The eight shadow-direction clusters and flat-surface placement constraints further limit the simulated realism.

The SVDS component is thin: a two-level denoising-strength schedule with a hand-picked 0.99 threshold, presented as a named contribution. No sensitivity analysis of the threshold is given, and its ablation gains over DS=0.99 (Table 2d vs f) are within a small range.

Some presentation issues reduce confidence: the abstract/intro promise 'adaptive' attention, but ATA is a fixed supervised loss with no adaptive mechanism beyond standard attention; Fig. 6 reports attention-map 'recall' of 0.97 with no precision, which is uninformative when attention maps are diffuse; and the user study protocol (30 participants, per-method forced choice) is described only at a high level without statistical testing.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: explicitly separating and supervising object vs. object-effect regions (shadows, reflections) addresses a genuine weakness of prior inpainting/removal methods, and the ATA attention supervision (Eq. 2) is a simple but sensible mechanism for this.

The OBER dataset is a meaningful community contribution: a hybrid of 2,715 counterfactually captured pairs plus a principled simulation pipeline (alpha maps via Eq. 1, lighting-direction clustering, multi-object compositing), with fine-grained object and object-effect masks and a stated public release promise. Table 4 clearly positions it against existing datasets.

Evaluation breadth is unusually thorough: RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild, plus external benchmarks (OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, MULAN) in the supplement, with both quantitative metrics, a 30-person user study, and qualitative comparisons under two mask conditions.

The authors proactively address the most obvious fairness objection — that Attention-Guided Fusion is a copy-paste-style blending advantage — in Sec. 8.3/Table 7, showing ObjectClear still leads when all baselines are given ground-truth object-effect masks for blending. The ablation (Table 2) cleanly isolates contributions of ATA, simulated data, AGF, and SVDS.
Reasonable efficiency argument (SDXL-based, ~5x faster than Flux-based OmniPaint/OmniEraser) and an honest limitations section (Fig. 17) on overlapping shadow disentanglement.
weaknesses: The headline quantitative margins on OBER-Test (e.g., 33.04 PSNR vs. 29.06 for OmniPaint) are partially circular: OBER-Test is drawn from the same capture and simulation pipeline used for training, so the model is evaluated on in-distribution data while baselines are not. The external-benchmark gains are smaller and more credible, which the paper's framing could acknowledge more explicitly.

AGF fundamentally relies on copying the input background back over the generated output; the paper argues this is an integral design rather than post-processing, but this makes the strong PSNR/PSNR-BG numbers partly a property of blending rather than generation quality. The Table 7 control mitigates but does not fully remove this concern, since the baseline 'w/b' blending uses a hard GT mask rather than a comparable soft predicted mask.

SVDS is a thin contribution: applying DS=1.0 inside the mask and DS=0.99 outside is a minor engineering heuristic, and the 0.99 value for the background is described as empirical without sensitivity analysis.

Some evaluation details are underspecified: the threshold defining the object-effect mask from pixel differences is not given, ReMOVE† is a custom modification of an existing metric evaluated only on OBER-Wild (where no GT exists), and the OBER-Test set of 163 samples is small, making large PSNR gaps sensitive to a few outliers.

The alpha-map formula in Eq. 1 and the simulation pipeline have edge cases (e.g., pixels where Igt < Iin due to noise, negative alpha) that are not discussed; the claimed physical plausibility of simulated shadows/reflections is asserted rather than validated quantitatively.

Attention-map quality is characterized only by recall (~0.97 in Fig. 6); precision or IoU against the GT effect mask would better establish that AGF blending is not overwriting too much of the generated content.
